https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.text:
Last September, when Queen Elizabeth II died, Alan Titchmarsh was worried he might lose touch with his old friend Charles. The 74-year-old gardener feared the King would have less time and perhaps less freedom to socialise. “Becoming king is a huge responsibility, so I had no expectations,” Titchmarsh says. “But I have seen him and we’ve written to each other a few times. I can’t exactly grill him or say, ‘Oi, how’s it going?’ but I think he’s doing very well. He and the Queen have grown into their roles and I sense an ease to them both.
“As Prince of Wales, he was ahead of his time, talking about the importance of the environment, and I think people see he is a man of our time.” On the day we speak Greenpeace protesters have climbed up the prime minister Rishi Sunak’s Yorkshire home (he was away), Just Stop Oil protesters have disrupted another sports event and wildfires are ripping through southern Europe.
Titchmarsh and the King share a passion for the environment. Do he and Charles approve of direct action? “I think the right to protest is very important,” he says. “I hope these activists who are throwing paint over pictures in the National Portrait Gallery are going home and planting something or taking care of bees. Because you can’t just protest — you have to actively cultivate whatever your little patch is too.”
What about the King? Does he privately have a sneaking admiration for those taking a radical approach? “I couldn’t possibly comment. That’s for him to say. But as a man of the land, I think we need to distinguish between climate and weather. I’m not a climate-change denier but there are natural variables. We’ve had a washout of the summer here in the UK when, after last year’s high temperatures, many predicted we’d have a tropical climate permanently.”
Titchmarsh is more adaptable than any gardening multitool. A former apprentice council gardener in Ilkley, Yorkshire, he is the same affable everyman at a formal dinner with the royal family or discussing bone meal with regular punters he meets in the street. It’s what made him a star on the BBC’s Gardeners’ World, Songs of Praise and countless other TV shows where a Middle England pin-up was required. His ease in all social settings informs his new book, Chatsworth: The Gardens and the People Who Made Them , a lavish tome celebrating the Derbyshire home of the Devonshire family. Chatsworth has just changed hands: William and Laura, the Earl and Countess of Burlington, have taken over from his parents, Peregrine, aka Stoker, and Amanda, the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire. The 35,000-acre estate boasts some of the finest gardens in the UK, although Titchmarsh has never worked on them. He’s a family friend. One of his heroes, the 18th-century gardener Capability Brown, created an Arcadian idyll here in 1758 and there are more than a few comparisons between the two.
“Brown was from humble beginnings, yet as comfortable around kings and queens and prime ministers as with the Irish navvies who worked for him,” Titchmarsh says, beaming. “He was not overwhelmed by grandeur and not too snooty to talk to people he might have considered below him on the social spectrum, and it strikes me that’s a good outlook to have. I’m not a social climber but I meet these people and we just get on. I’ve never earned the sort of money Brown did, though — he had earned the equivalent of £500 million by the time he died.”
As a family friend (Titchmarsh first met Deborah, the former Duchess of Devonshire and the youngest of the society celebrities the Mitford sisters, after being sent to interview her in the Eighties) he has been entrusted to tell the Chatsworth story. Some of his own experiences with the Devonshires sound extraordinary. In 2005 he and his wife, Alison, were guests at one of their other estates, the 33,000 acres of Bolton Abbey in North Yorkshire. Other dinner guests included Queen Elizabeth II, the Duke of Edinburgh and the Princess Royal. During dinner Titchmarsh pointed out that his father, a plumber, had installed the lead roof on the abbey.
“The Princess Royal put down her cutlery, raised an eyebrow and said, ‘Well, thank goodness he didn’t take it off,’ ” Titchmarsh says with a chuckle. I’m not sure why this is funny, but it seems the Princess Royal was grateful Titchmarsh Sr hadn’t stolen the lead. A bit rude if you ask me. “It was a joke,” he insists. “She’s quite sharp. That’s the thing. You just find that common bit of warmth and humanity and everyone gets along.”
Titchmarsh has a soft spot for the high-born; you sense it in the way he recounts the recent tribulations of the aristocracy. The Devonshires enjoyed uninterrupted ownership of the stately home from 1553 until 1950. When the 10th Duke of Devonshire died suddenly, the family was hit with a huge inheritance tax bill. Selling parts of the estate and opening it to the public saved it. Recounting this, Titchmarsh refers to the death duties bill as “punitive” and “crippling”. Does he disapprove of inheritance tax?
“When you think about it, all we earn has already been taxed. I earn a decent whack. I’m not on me uppers but I’m not outrageously wealthy. I’m comfortable. I will have to pay inheritance tax but a part of me does think, ‘I’ve already paid.’ It’s a difficult one because I accept that’s how we operate as a country. I’m not one to featherbed because then I think your children lose their sense of purpose, but I do want to leave something for them.”
Chatsworth is open to the public, hosts lots of events and attracts more than half a million visitors a year. Titchmarsh insists that it has all turned out for the best because the family enjoy welcoming people to their home. “They love sharing it,” he says. “When a visitor once jumped into the lake, someone complained and Debo said, ‘Isn’t it wonderful!’ You get snooty landowners who say things like, ‘The general public smell rather strange,’ but I’ve never heard any of that at Chatsworth.”
The 105 acres of gardens are tended by an expert team assisted by a small army of volunteers. It struck me as slightly feudal how one minute we’re reading about the plucky “people’s team” (some are paid, some aren’t) and the next hearing about rooms full of Rembrandts and Hockneys.
“But they’re there for all to see,” he insists. “And don’t forget the family spotted talents like Hockney and Lucian Freud early in their careers — they didn’t buy these works at the top of the market. Freud was very adept at sucking up to the aristocracy so he enjoyed it too. Besides, I’m not one of those who feels, ‘Well, if I can’t have it, then no one else can.’ I started out as a council gardener on £3 a week. If you start minding people having more than you, then you’re on the way to communism — maybe that’s what you are?”
Ouch. I can’t be a communist, I’ve got an Isa. But his book sounds elegiac about the great houses. Doesn’t Chatsworth’s story signal the inevitable fate of, say, Buckingham Palace? “Parts of Buckingham Palace are already open, of course, but who knows? The trick is not to traduce their grandeur and history. Longleat and Woburn tried it with safari parks. One has to innovate without losing the charm and magic.”
Titchmarsh is fundamentally decent, centrist, always wanting to see both sides. That’s why when he takes a firm view it makes headlines. Recently he caused a stir when he told a House of Lords investigation into rewilding that the practice was catastrophic for biodiversity. “It has been wrongly promulgated that rewilding ensures maximum biodiversity,” he says. “That’s wrong. A well-cultivated garden will give you even more. But, as in most things, the answer is a balance; I have a two-acre wildflower meadow, so I’m not against it per se.”
● Alan Titchmarsh: Rewilding is a catastrophe for wildlife
He similarly caught flak when he said that he didn’t use a power mower or a leaf blower on Sunday mornings so that he didn’t disturb neighbours in the Hampshire village where he lives. Some saw this as Titchmarsh flaunting his privilege. After all, it was pointed out on social media, some people only have Sunday to mow the lawn. “I totally understand that and I don’t judge others,” he says with a sigh. “We are such an angry country sometimes. People don’t want to listen to what I actually said. They just attack, which is a pity.”
He sounds a bit weary and, he says, sometimes he feels guilty. Guilty, for example, because buying a house is so hard for young people. There are plans to put up a housing development in his village. Is he a nimby? “No, but when you’ve got young families who’ve already moved there to give their children access to woodland, are you going to deprive them? You can’t concrete over everything, but then again people have got to live somewhere — it’s very difficult.”
This is boomer guilt, I suggest. The novelist Ian McEwan put it well. A year older than Titchmarsh, McEwan said his generation ate all the “cream”: no wars to fight in, the birth of rock’n’roll and free love, plentiful housing and mass travel; the younger generation are angry they’ll never have it as good.
When I put this to him, Titchmarsh doesn’t sound quite so beleaguered. “You can’t choose when you’re born, can you? I left school at 15 with one O-level. My first wage was £3 a week and my first mortgage attracted 14 per cent interest. When we were first married my wife and I had to save up for a Christmas joint [he means meat]. It was no bed of roses; it was hard work but we got stuck in. The worst thing is moaning. The world doesn’t owe you a living.”
Chatsworth is what you get from the “best endeavours” of fair-minded people working together with the community, he says. It’s a beautiful estate that might have been lost to the nation but which has found a place in the modern world through creativity and compromise. “The locals love it and the Devonshires love the locals,” he says. I ask him what his next project is and he says he’s about to start on his 12th novel. Queen Elizabeth once applauded him for giving “a lot of ladies a lot of pleasure” and it looks like he is still very much dedicated to this task. “It’s about a city widow who pitches up in the countryside to find herself again,” he says. “I promise I’m not trying to start trouble but I’m thinking of calling it The Rewilding of Rosie.”Chatsworth by Alan Titchmarsh (Ebury £35). https://www.thetimes.com/article/japan-t.title: Japan to pump 1m tonnes of Fukushima water into sea
https://www.thetimes.com/article/japan-t.subtitle: Nuclear plant still decades away from safe dismantling after 2011 tsunami
https://www.thetimes.com/article/japan-t.text:
Japan will begin pumping more than a million tonnes of contaminated water from the Fukushima nuclear power plant into the Pacific Ocean on Thursday, provoking opposition from fishermen and the country’s neighbours.
The water will be released into the sea over 30 years. It has been treated and diluted to remove most radioactive contaminants, but the wastewater will still contain traces of the radioactive isotope tritium.
“I have asked Tepco [Tokyo Electric Power Company] to swiftly prepare for the water discharge in accordance with the plan approved by the Nuclear Regulation Authority, and expect the water release to start on 24 August, weather conditions permitting,” Fumio Kishida, the Japanese prime minister, said.
The announcement comes two days after Kishida visited local fishermen, who he said expressed “a degree of understanding” over the water release. “I promise that we will take on the entire responsibility of ensuring the fishing industry can continue to make their living, even if that will take decades,” Kishida said.
Twelve years after a tsunami caused the meltdown of three of its reactors, the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant is still decades away from being safely dismantled. In the meantime, it continues to contaminate more than 150 tonnes of water every day.
Some of this is poured directly onto the broken reactors to cool them. Much is natural groundwater that flows through the earth towards the sea, picking up radiation on the way.
The plant’s operator, Tepco, pumps out the irradiated water and stores it in more than 1000 huge storage tanks — 1.36 million tonnes so far.
In theory, filtering can remove all the radioactive elements except for tritium, which is routinely released into the sea in diluted form from nuclear plants around the world. But trace elements of more dangerous radioactive substances, including strontium-90 and iodine-129, have also been detected in the water.
“We are deeply disappointed and outraged by the Japanese government’s announcement to release water containing radioactive substances into the ocean despite concerns raised by fishermen, citizens, Fukushima residents and the international community,” Hisayo Takada, of Greenpeace Japan, said.
The leader of Hong Kong, John Lee, said on Tuesday he strongly opposed Japan’s plan to release the wastewater and that he had instructed the city’s government to “immediately activate” import control measures on Japanese seafood.
The tritium will be diluted to less than one-40th of the concentration permitted under Japanese safety standards and one-seventh of the World Health Organization’s permitted level for safe drinking water. The discharge of the water is supported by the International Atomic Energy Agency, which predicts a “negligible radiological impact on people and the environment”.
Opposition to the plan from Pacific island nations and South Korea has diminished in recent months but China remains highly critical. However, Japanese officials say that Chinese nuclear power plants routinely discharge levels of tritium well above those that will be pumped from Fukushima and that Beijing is using the controversy for political ends.
Wang Wenbin, the Chinese foreign ministry spokesman, said: “China strongly insists that Japan should rectify this wrong decision and abandon its plan to discharge radioactive water into the sea. If this radioactive water is safe, there is no need to dump it into the sea.”

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/letters.title: Bicycling busybodies are the real danger on the road
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/letters.text:
“Cycling Mikey”, Mike van Erp, is proud of having caught 1,400 drivers using their phones (“Smile! You’re on camera”, Magazine, last week). But what is the logic of a law that potentially loses someone their livelihood because they use a phone when stationary, in a jam, with the engine switched off, but does not punish a self-appointed busybody from engaging that driver in conversation through the car window?
And when the traffic moves again, who will be the greater danger to other road users: the driver who just used the phone, or the driver who used the phone, was harangued by a sneak, and now realises they may lose their licence and job? Michael Stannard, Verbier, Switzerland
Please could “Cyling Mikey” use his head camera to capture law-breaking cyclists — such as the one recently who was riding illegally on the pavement, eyes on their phone, and then swung out directly in front of my car without looking up?
Fortunately, I managed to swerve and avoid a collision. But must we now drive in the middle of the road to save the lives of these uninsured lunatics?Mike Dunstan, Woodley, Reading
Motorists are angels compared with cyclists, who are generally a menace. My commute is a walk across the City of London, and I’ve lost count of how many near-misses I’ve had from cyclists riding on pavements or running red lights.Michael Osborne, London SE1
Mikey and his admirer Jeremy Vine are both happy to harass motorists. I hope they would also support a call for all bicycles and e-scooters to be licensed, and then do the same to those riding them?Alan Brown, East Molesey, Surrey
The negative reaction to “Cycling Mikey” can be summed up thus: “I know I am breaking the law but I am offended that you are submitting evidence of my law-breaking to the justice system.”
Van Erp is not applying points to people’s licences, fining them or causing loss of employment. The justice system does that, if there is clear evidence they have broken the law. Rather, he is simply acting in the best interests of society and other road users.Norman Boyes, Waterlooville, Hampshire
I was nearly knocked off my motorcycle by a car driver who was not looking at the road because he was on a mobile phone. It is no wonder feelings run high. Is texting a friend or checking your Facebook feed really more important than the safety of other road users?
I am no fan of vigilantes, but the vacuum left by the police was bound to be filled by self-appointed justice warriors. It seems the police are so busy defending the right of Just Stop Oil to ruin people’s lives that they do not have time to check for errant mobile phone usage.Jolyon de Fossard, Pampanga, The Philippines
Van Erp is highlighting crimes that may result in death or serious injury. Drivers should not check their phone even if stationary. While concentrating on the phone, traffic can move on: drivers look up, notice, hurriedly engage gear and pull off — and at such moments hit someone they did not see earlier, as their attention was elsewhere.David Allison, Paphos, Cyprus
Given the rules on mobile phones, why are car companies making their vehicles so reliant on central touchscreens? They are dangerous to use, taking your eyes off the road every time. It would be safer to go back to knobs and buttons.Mike Hughes, Eskdale, Lake District
Van Erp is doing a good job of persuading people that road rules are there to be obeyed, but as a keen cyclist myself, I was disappointed by what I saw in the photos. Why does he not wear a helmet?Amanda Jones, St Peter Port, Guernsey

https://www.thetimes.com/article/a-rigge.title: A rigged system: why North Sea oil workers fear for their future
https://www.thetimes.com/article/a-rigge.text:
Jordan Flett was 18 when he first set foot on an oil rig. The rig floorman, or “roughneck”, is now 29, a tall, stocky, bearded figure with a habit of leaning back in his chair to pause and stare, as if at distant horizons. Joining the industry was “quite intimidating”, he says, and not because of the fast-paced and often dangerous work, which he had experienced on building sites. What’s special about a rig is the isolated community of some 130 men, mostly much older than him, living and working together on 12-hour shifts, seven days a week, for three weeks at a time. The first three days after a break are the worst, he says, when memories of home are still fresh. But then you settle in.
The rig I meet Flett on is a $550 million, 32,000-tonne “jack-up” in Dundee harbour, which has 170-metre “legs” that crank down at sea and up in port. The living quarters can house 128 men in double cabins: while one man sleeps, the other works. But nowadays there are leisure facilities too: wifi, a pool table and big TV, a decent canteen, and underfloor heating in the bathrooms (though no sauna, unlike on most Nordic rigs). There are poker nights, the main currency on a rig being “juice and a sweetie”, as one of Flett’s colleagues puts it. And there is the pleasure of seeing whales and dolphins pass by and watching sunrises and sunsets over a boundless horizon.
Eleven years into his career, Flett has a wife and two children, aged four and two, to take care of. He missed his son’s birthday for work recently but he has no doubt about whether the oil business is worth it: “It’s been good to our family.” His father worked in the industry, as did his stepfather. The attraction is obvious: after the three weeks on, rig workers get three full weeks off. And the industry pays well: about £70,000 a year for a roughneck like Flett, rising to over £140,000 for a driller and more than £190,000 for an offshore installation manager (OIM), the most senior role on a rig.
It is exactly this livelihood and all the associated benefits to the UK that Rishi Sunak has said he wants to sustain by handing out more than 100 new oil and gas licences. Even though its production has peaked, steady investment could keep the North Sea producing for decades, securing jobs, improving British energy security and, by mitigating the need for more carbon-intensive imports, cutting European emissions by millions of tonnes, according to Wood Mackenzie, a research firm. Oil and gas supply 69 per cent of UK energy needs and most of that still comes from domestic production. Without the North Sea, Britain will simply have to import more, even under a net-zero scenario.
Yet despite Sunak’s warm words this week, a visit to Aberdeen, Dundee and Grangemouth reveals an industry in trouble. While oil and gas investment is taking off around the world, Britain is stuck on the sidelines thanks to the introduction of a punitive windfall tax last year and Labour’s threat to put a stop to all new development if it wins power. Instead of getting bigger, much of the North Sea industry is spiralling into decline, sending waves of anxiety through the communities based around it.
In May last year, Sunak added a supposedly temporary 25 per cent surcharge to the 40 per cent tax on UK oil and gas profits. In November, after the mini budget, this was increased to 35 per cent and extended until 2028, regardless of oil prices. The oil majors, which produce a fraction of their profits in the UK, absorbed it, but the effect on national production and investment was stark. Activity dropped to a 40-year low and lay-offs quickly followed.
Rigs like Flett’s should be out at sea working to open new fields such as Rosebank and Cambo, which Wood Mackenzie estimates would be worth £40 billion to the UK economy. Instead, Ithaca Energy has put those projects on hold and rigs are sitting in port between short-term jobs or, worse, being towed away to more lucrative oil basins. The men (and few women) who work in the industry believe that once they’re gone, they will never return.
Outside Aberdeen, in a business park of low-rise office blocks plonked in green fields and forested hills, a group of anxious men has gathered. They are from firms belonging to the International Association of Drilling Companies (IADC), a global industry group for businesses that provide services such as drilling and equipment to oil production companies. Unlike oil producers, which reap windfalls when prices rise, drillers bear the huge risk of paying to build rigs while collecting a far thinner margin once they are in operation. In the UK, the association’s members employ 3,000 people.
But UK drillers are struggling. British producers, blindsided by their tax burden rising to 75 per cent, are offering them only £100,000-£150,000 a day to rent rigs on short jobs for a few months, versus rates of £450,000 a day for long-term contracts elsewhere. A whole group of drillers — Diamond, Valaris, Noble and Seadrill — were only just emerging from Covid-induced bankruptcies. Now many are in layoff mode yet again. The men running these businesses, usually stoic, media-shy and practical problem-solvers, are worried.
“The cycle has stopped,” says Darren Sutherland, vice-president at Borr Drilling. The other seven men, six Scottish and one English, agree. Unlike the other oil price busts, this one has been brought about not by a falling oil price, but by government action.
Nearly all of the men began their careers as roughnecks like Flett and climbed the ranks to earn salaries north of £150,000. For most of them, oil runs in the family. Sutherland, who met his wife in Venezuela on an oil job (her father and grandfather were also in oil), has a son who only started on a rig a year ago, but his father fears he’ll have to go abroad to stay in the industry. “I’m really, really proud to be a driller and to be a driller from the North Sea,” he says. “It’s painful to see it disappear in front of you. I get emotional.” Abruptly, he struggles to speak. Paul Brown of Rig Surveys Group, agrees, shaking his head as he thinks of “all that knowledge and experience just gone”.
Politicians like to talk of “green jobs” filling the gap, but no one I meet sees that as an immediate prospect. Instead, skills in the oil industry that might be adapted to build carbon-capture facilities or floating wind farms will be lost as redundancies and recruitment freezes erode the workforce. Aberdeen’s economy has changed before, of course, from fishing to paper to granite, yet there was always overlap. “This time, there doesn’t seem to be an overlap,” says Sandy Milne, who does not wish his employer to be named.
As for climate change, a couple of the drillers voice scepticism about the evidence, but the rest say they believe in the theory and the need to change, just not the practicalities of the net-zero agenda. “I believe it’s real,” Sutherland says, but the energy transition needs to be implemented “in a timely and structured manner”.
As we walk to the car, I look around. In 2012, the drillers tell me, it was hard to find parking here. Now, dozens of the offices are empty and the few cars stand out in the empty lots. As Ray Taylor, one of the drillers, puts it, if oil goes, “What’s Aberdeen going to turn to?”
Strolling through Aberdeen’s West End is a tour of wealth and respectability. There are rows of well-tended roses and lavender bushes, bright green lawns filled with figurines and even one boasting a mini putting green. The large, granite houses are a mix of homes and offices — drilling consultancies, wealth managers and private nurseries or schools. But even here, the number of “To Let” signs is multiplying. A short walk away, on Aberdeen’s main thoroughfare, Union Street, you pass one empty shop after another. “I’ve never seen it like this,” says Stuart Clow, an IADC director, who was born nearby.
Duncan Massey, a local oil consultant, was so incensed by the state of the city after Covid and the cutting off of recovery by the windfall tax that he decided to stand for election. He became Conservative councillor for Lower Deeside last year. So far, he says, the green jobs on offer are “small beer” and he worries that his children will have to leave Aberdeen: “Are there going to be enough opportunities for them to stay?” he wonders, citing how few people wind farms employ. “If there’s 20,000 energy transition jobs in the whole of Scotland I’d be surprised.” That compares with 200,000 employed in the UK oil and gas supply chain.
Voters who want the oil industry to thrive have few options. The SNP used to support it: in the 2014 independence referendum, oil revenues were a key part of the fiscal plan. But now, in coalition with the Greens at Holyrood, the SNP has flip-flopped on whether it will allow more development. And Labour under Sir Keir Starmer has said it would stop all new fields, creating a huge dampener on investment. All of this is despite the Climate Change Committee concluding last year that UK producers have “a relatively low carbon footprint” compared to imports and that ending new production would send a “signal” rather than actually delivering a “clear-cut” reduction.
Sunak’s announcement this week is one bright spot in an otherwise bleak landscape. But it would take three years from new licences being granted to the drillers feeling the benefit. And after years of political attacks, Clow is cautious. “Let’s hope there is noU-turn,” he says.
A hundred miles south of Aberdeen lies Grangemouth Refinery, a 1,700-acre complex of pipes, chimneys, and siloes that is responsible for refining 70 per cent of Scotland’s petrol and diesel fuel. The 100-year-old refinery, owned jointly by Ineos and PetroChina, employs 1,300 people with an average salary of £36,000. The day I visit the area, Just Stop Oil has just been cleared out, but feelings are raw.
In a nail salon in the depressingly empty shopping centre of Grangemouth, where paint is peeling from the signposts, a woman with a glimmering red manicure lets rip at the protesters’ demands but will not give her name. “Shut down Ineos?” she exclaims. “That would be devastating for Grangemouth.” Her husband, her son and her niece all work at the refinery and she is furious, especially at protesters glueing themselves to the roof.
Gerry McCafferty is a worker at the plant. We meet in a Falkirk café near a busy cinema where pink-clad girls are streaming in to see the Barbie movie. “It’s a good standard of living,” he says. His father worked at Grangemouth; so does his brother, and he hopes one of his daughters might go into it one day. McCafferty commutes to the job to work 12-hour shifts seven days a week from 40 minutes away in Glasgow.
He takes a friendlier attitude to Just Stop Oil — “they’re genuinely nice people” — but disagrees with them firmly: “The thought of it stopping tomorrow morning or any day in the near future is catastrophic . . . There is probably not a family in this town [that] doesn’t have someone working there.” Nor will the workers let the industry die without a fight. McCafferty is a member of the GMB union, a Labour Party paymaster, and a vocal opponent of Starmer’s North Sea plan. He also opposes the windfall tax. Politicians, he said, “are killing us . . . taxing us to death”.
The oil industry is a source of shared history and pride as well as income. North Sea oil production took off in the late 1970s and in 1984 produced peak tax revenues equal to 30 per cent of GDP.
Brian Winton, the general manager at Ithaca, was a farmer’s son who began as an apprentice at British Steel — the sort of career path that many politicians now eulogise. He proudly shows me all the rigs he helped to build. “Not many people in Aberdeen have built this infrastructure and this infrastructure,” he says. The industry has kept his family together: he has two sons working in oil and six grandchildren living nearby.
The growth was not without a price, however. In Hazlehead Park, Clow shows me the monument commemorating the Piper Alpha disaster, the worst in the history of offshore oil. In 1988, the rig was engulfed in a fireball inadvertently fed by gas pumped by the next-door rig; 165 men died. One of them had been a friend and a regular at the pub where Clow worked. “There he is,” Clow says, finding his name on the stone. “How old was he?” he asks himself. The answer: 21.
In those days, it was common to lose fingers screwing pipes together, rigs could come unanchored and tip over in 100ft waves and, in riskier regions, tales of kidnappings are still common. Older drillers recall a culture of helicopter rides accompanied by cigarettes and death metal music, and a strict hierarchy in which no one dared start the post-shift film before the chief driller (or “drill daddy”) was ready.
Piper Alpha precipitated new safety standards, subsequently introduced across the world. There are now protocols to avoid dropping objects from heights, rig “red zones” policed by alarms and even rules for going up and down stairs. The latest addition is a new mental health charter: young men are most at risk of suicide and it is a significant cause of death on rigs. Many older workers have been on teams that have lost men. The IADC’s safety awards, a huge, black-tie dinner, are a major event in the Aberdeen social calendar. Last year, a rock pipe band called the Red Hot Chilli Pipers played.
Not everywhere operates to the same standards, however. At Ithaca’s offices, Willie Watt, turnaround team leader and a father of four, shows me pictures from a stint he spent years ago on a cockroach-infested rig in west Africa. One day, he was astonished to see a geyser of oil shooting out of the water. A boat was sent to set it alight and the fiery pool floated off, thankfully not in his direction. “The imports we’re taking are from processes like that,” he says. “Even if we shut down the North Sea, these places are still going. Here, if we drop a teaspoon of oil, we have to report it and we do.”
Yet there is a broad sense of frustration at the way the industry is portrayed. “There is a perception that we’re the bad guys,” Paul Brown says. Steve Baylis, a crane operator on the same rig as Flett, says: “I consider myself a green person. I recycle . . . I paid for solar panels.” Yet, as Sandy Milne puts it: “We’re being ignored.” For an industry of practical, highly trained people whose skills will be needed to build any kind of green energy system, it stings.
Kim Beattie, a graduate trainee at Ithaca, has just begun her career in oil. A graduate of Aberdeen University, she looked for “green jobs”, but 90 per cent of the roles on offer were in oil and gas. Now, however, she wants to stay in the industry. “I don’t know if this will exist in 20 years,” she says, “but I hope it does.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: We’ll lose seats if Rishi Sunak dilutes net zero, warn blue wall Tories
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Rishi Sunak is facing a backlash from blue wall Tory MPs who have said that he will cost them their seats at the next election if he panders to the right of the party on climate change and human rights commitments.
A group representing about 150 Tories has told Sunak to ignore the “siren voices” of those pressing him to water down net-zero targets.
Downing Street has signalled that the government is looking at scaling down its push for net zero because of the financial pressure on households during the cost of living crisis.
But Chris Skidmore, the MP for Kingswood and former net-zero tsar, said: “Net zero is no longer just about the environment, critical though that is. The vital importance of net zero is whether you understand the economies of the future and want the UK to lead and succeed in these, or be condemned to following, to missing out, on these opportunities and costing the UK and local communities jobs and economic growth.”
Downing Street is also under pressure from several dozen Tory MPs over suggestions by Robert Jenrick, the immigration minister, that the government could pull out of the European Convention of Human Rights if it attempts to block the government’s Rwanda deportation scheme.
Jenrick told Times Radio the government would “do whatever is necessary” to ensure the plans went ahead even if it lost a Supreme Court challenge expected in autumn.
But one senior Tory MP said No 10 had been warned against any move to pull out of the convention saying it would “play into the hands of the Lib Dems” in dozens of seats that the party needed to win at the next election.
“It would be completely self-destructive,” the MP said. “A lot of colleagues are very nervous. It might play well on the right but among the voters we need to win to hold our seats in the south it just plays into the hands of the Lib Dems. It is wrong-headed and bad politics.”
• Will climate change and energy commitments be watered down?
Among those Tories who have concerns is the former deputy prime minister Damian Green, chairman of the One Nation group of Tory centrist MPs. He said that pulling out of the European Convention on Human Rights would not change the English court’s views so it would be ineffective in toughening asylum policy but would have other damaging consequences both for the UK and the Tory party. “It would seriously damage our international standing. It would be bad policy and bad politics as it would alienate moderate Conservative voters,” he said.
The plan is also opposed by a number of senior government figures including Alex Chalk, the justice secretary, and Victoria Prentis, the attorney-general.
Tories on the right of the party have also urged Sunak to review the deadlines around environmental measures after voter concerns about the expansion of London’s ultra low emission zone helped the party to hang on to the Uxbridge & South Ruislip seat at last month’s by-election.
• The Ulez lesson: voters like eco policies as long as they cost net zero
The result has given the Tories hope that its chances of pulling off a shock general election victory are not over if it can focus on issues where there is a clear divide with Labour.
Sunak said he was committed to tackling climate change but also approved the issuing of hundreds of new oil and gas licences for the North Sea, and declared himself “on the side of motorists”.
The Tories have also tried to link extreme groups such as Just Stop Oil with the Labour Party for political gain.
Last week George Eustice, the former environment secretary, said a proposed ban on oil boilers should be delayed because of the cost to rural households.
Yesterday a relaunched Tory pressure group warned ministers against pursuing “more extreme” net-zero policies. The Conservative Rural Forum, made up of grassroots activists, was revived amid fears of Conservative prospects in the countryside.
Lizzie Hacking, its chairwoman, said: “Everyone does want net zero, but perhaps some of the asks of other groups are slightly more extreme than what the majority of the public wants.”
But Derek Thomas, the Tory MP for St Ives, said that although “many rural communities have no choice but to use expensive oil to heat their homes” this meant the government should be more ambitious in its schemes.
He said: “Reaching net zero should be an opportunity to cut their bills while tackling climate change. That’s why it’s so essential the government offers grants to fuel-poor homes for insulation and heat pumps and looks at incentives like stamp duty cuts to help people pay for home upgrades.
“It’s right we debate how we achieve our goals but voters don’t want to see us backtrack on climate change.”
Siobhan Baillie, the Conservative MP for Stroud, said: “Ambitious green policies that cut bills and create jobs are an electoral asset, not a liability.”
Jo Gideon, the Conservative MP for Stoke-on-Trent Central, said: “With global competition intensifying we should accelerate our efforts, not backtrack.”
She said minimising costs was key “but we shouldn’t wave the white flag when we could be trailblazers for the next Industrial Revolution”.
Sam Hall, director of the Conservative Environment Network, which has the backing of more than 150 Tory parliamentarians and 400 councillors, said: “While a few loud siren voices within the Conservative movement want to ditch net zero, they are in the minority.
“Overwhelmingly Conservative MPs and the party’s voters support climate action to protect the environment for future generations, attract new industries and strengthen our energy security. Few votes can be won by rolling back on green targets, but many could be lost.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/zadie-s.title: Why Zadie Smith is the voice of the 21st century
https://www.thetimes.com/article/zadie-s.text:
This article was first published on August 16
There’s a telling moment in Zadie Smith’s new historical novel, The Fraud, in which the real-life Victorian novelist William Ainsworth gives his opinion on Middlemarch by the new literary upstart George Eliot. Virginia Woolf famously called Middlemarch “one of the few English novels written for grown-up people” and it’s fair to say it has aged better than any of Ainsworth’s 41 terrible books, wildly successful in their day.
The eminent man of letters cannot see the appeal, though. “No adventure, no drama, no murder, nothing to excite the blood or chill it!” he complains. “Is this all that these modern ladies’ novels are to be about? People?”
“I like it,” his housekeeper, Eliza Touchet, counters, concealing a smile — and you can imagine Zadie Smith doing the same.
People, Smith has always insisted, whether implicitly in novels such as On Beauty or Swing Time, or explicitly in her essays, are the most interesting thing of all. There are few 21st-century English novelists who take such a relentless interest in our multitudes: our comedies and tragedies, our bodies and minds, skin and teeth, blindnesses and hypocrisies, but also our moments of insight and grace and our reliable tendency to misunderstand and misinterpret one another — amplified in our shrill, algorithmic age.
It might seem a little premature to award the Sunday Times Award for Literary Excellence to an author not yet 50 (she is 47), but Smith’s career is already as old as the century and, I hate to break it to you, that century is now getting on a bit. Her debut, White Teeth, arrived in January 2000 when Smith was 24. Had she been a less precocious age she would be in her late-middle age by now and it would seem an entirely appropriate moment to recognise a life’s work.
As it is she has spent more than half of her life as a published author, during which time she has written 12 books, ranging freely between fiction and non-fiction, realism and experimentation, autofiction, even sci-fi and now historical fiction — a departure she promised herself she would never make, as she wrote in a recent New Yorker essay. But she never claimed to be consistent.
“I’ve always been aware of being an inconsistent personality. Of having a lot of contradictory voices knocking around my head,” she wrote in one of her best essays, Fascinated to Presume, at once a defence of fiction and her right to imagine herself into whoever’s mind she pleases. Or as Eliza reflects in The Fraud, as she watches a speech by Andrew Bogle, the black former slave who is the closest thing that the novel has to a hero: “A person is a bottomless thing!”
Casting back, it’s hard to remember what an impact White Teeth made. Born Sadie — she added the Z at 14 in honour of the author Zora Neale Hurston — Smith had grown up poor but happy in a mixed-race family in a council house in Willesden, northwest London. Her parents split when she was young — her white father, Harvey, who was 30 years older than her mother, moved around the corner, and Zadie grew up with her mother Yvonne, a social worker of Jamaican heritage, and two younger brothers. She started writing her debut while a student at Cambridge University (where she met her husband, the Northern Irish poet Nick Laird) and it prompted a bidding war among publishers. Debuts are, typically, narrowly autobiographical. Here was a huge, multilayered and, yes, optimistic celebration of the multicultural London that had shaped Smith’s sensibility. “I’ll never forget [it]. The exuberance and energy of the writing were extraordinary — the words jumping off the page, the characters leaping into life,” her editor, Simon Prosser, said.
Readers adored it too. Smith won The Sunday Times Young Writer award and American critics took notice. The New York Times reviewer marvelled at a writer “who at the age of 24 demonstrates both an instinctive storytelling talent and a fully fashioned voice that’s street-smart and learned, sassy and philosophical all at the same time”.
● Zadie Smith: I couldn’t escape Charles Dickens — so I killed him
Sally Rooney is one of the few people who could empathise with being anointed the saviour of the novel in your early twenties. And Smith found herself cast in another unasked-for role: her dual British-Jamaican heritage and council estate-to-Cambridge trajectory held up as a feelgood tale for the early New Labour era. Smith wisely escaped the narrow London scene and moved to New York and often came across as dismissive of her earlier books. “It’s total self-disgust every time. I don’t keep any copies of my books in the house — they go to my mum’s flat. I don’t like them around,” she once told an interviewer. NW (2012) is far more pessimistic about working-class London life. The tensions and pretensions of black intellectual life formed one of the themes of On Beauty (2005).
Nevertheless, her success has been enabling for other writers with stories of different Britains to tell: Andrea Levy, Monica Ali, Hari Kunzru, Diana Evans et al. For all the inconsistency of subject, that voice remains consistent: wry, philosophical, questioning, as interested in Jay-Z’s flow or Ginger Rogers’s steps as she is in EM Forster’s morality or Kierkegaard’s philosophy.
In the intervening years Smith has moved in and out of fashion, the limelight and her beloved NW postcode —moving first to Rome, then to New York with Laird, where they brought up two children. But she has remained a champion of other writers and of fiction. Her ten-year spell teaching creative writing at NYU brought her into close contact with an emerging generation and placed her at the centre of the American literary scene.
And while existential doubt, parental anxieties and a darkening political awareness have crept into her work, there is an openness to new forms and modes of thinking — and a defiance of the narrow strictures of identity politics and social media (she is a staunch digital refusenik). After the death of her friend Martin Amis this year, it’s hard to think of a living essayist who is better company on the page — walking you through her thoughts, curious about everything and everyone, including (unusually) the reader.
In the introduction to her second essay collection, Feel Free (2018), she sets out her basic mode of essay writing. “I feel this — do you? I’m struck by this thought — are you?” And in her third collection, Intimations (2020), you’ll find the staunchest defence of fiction as the best place we have to defy the incuriosity and narrowness that have become hallmarks of the digital age. “The people we now cast into this place of non-interest were once the very people fiction was most curious about. The conflicted, the liars, the self-deceiving, the wilfully blind, the abject, the unresolved, the imperfect, the evil, the unwell, the lost and divided.”
All these qualities are evident in The Fraud, which is historical fiction done in the most Zadie Smith way possible. (“Because this is the other thing about immigrants,” she wrote in White Teeth. “They cannot escape their history any more than you yourself can lose your shadow.”)
All of William Ainsworth’s criticisms might apply: Smith has never really been one for plot or adventure. It is inconsistent in time and tone. And it is a novel that does not announce its great theme — slavery — although it affects everything that the characters experience, so vast it almost cannot be seen.
● Ten of the best essay collections — from Martin Amis to Zadie Smith
The novel is also about deception. The fraud of the title is the fabled Tichborne Claimant, the poor butcher from Wapping who claimed to be the long-lost heir to a vast fortune and became a populist hero. But everyone in it is a fraud in some way, including the former slave Bogle, who might have been an African prince were his father not abducted and taken to Jamaica. And those on what we would call the right side of history — the abolitionists and campaigners — also have their blindnesses and hypocrisies, much as Just Stop Oil protesters and Black Lives Matter activists do today.
Not that Smith is judging. “It has become the fashion for novelists to dictate to their readers, to tell them which characters to respect and which to despise, whom to love and whom to admire, whom to fear and whom to befriend,” she writes in an accompanying essay. “I prefer to think of readers making their own judgments, fierce or sympathetic as the case may be. That’s the kind of reader I am.”
So, nothing to excite the blood or chill it — beyond all the participants in the human comedy of life.Zadie Smith appears at Cheltenham Literature Festival on October 13 at 8.30pm. The Fraud is published on September 7 (Hamish Hamilton £20). Buy from timesbookshop.co.uk or call 020 3176 2935. Discount for Times+ members
Smith’s breezy, boisterous debut novel about multicultural London delighted readers when it appeared. Following several mixed-race families, it leaps back and forth in time between 1945 and the 1990s, offering multiple perspectives on the immigrant’s experience of assimilation. The novel revealed Smith’s great range — and became an instant bestseller.
Shortlisted for the 2005 Booker prize, Smith’s third novel (which is loosely based on EM Forster’s Howards End) is a culture-clash comedy tackling issues of class, politics and morality. Set in an American liberal arts college, it traces the intertwined lives of two families, the conservative, British-Trinidadian Kipps and the more chaotic, British-American Belseys. It’s funny and unflinching.
Smith’s best novel, in my opinion, is complex, polyphonic, sexy (at times) and full of great social comedy. It is set in the same northwest London streets as White Teeth, where the writer grew up. The writing switches between stream of consciousness, first and third person and other styles.
This non-fiction collection’s 33 essays and columns reveal Smith’s terror of intellectual calcification. She wants her mind — and yours! — to stay supple. There’s something winning about her voice, cool but nerdy, open-minded but discerning as she ranges over subjects from Joni Mitchell to Jay-Z, Brexit to her childhood bathroom.
Launched in 1987 after Anthony Burgess was heard to complain that he had never received a prize (he became the first recipient), the Sunday Times Award for Literary Excellence has one of the most distinguished lists of alumni in the book world. Past winners have included Ted Hughes, Seamus Heaney, Muriel Spark, Harold Pinter, Anne Tyler, Margaret Atwood, Salman Rushdie, Ian McEwan, Kazuo Ishiguro, Julian Barnes, John le Carré, Sarah Waters, Tom Stoppard, Elena Ferrante and, last year, Stephen King.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.title: Before the Light Fades by Natasha Walter review — my family of activists
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.text:
In December 2017 Natasha Walter’s 75-year-old mother, Ruth, ordered a drug on the internet. She arranged her affairs, wrote farewell letters, got into bed and ended her life. She had not been depressed; she had simply decided, having noticed small memory lapses, that it was time to go.
Walter is a writer and human rights activist best known for her journalism, and her feminist books The New Feminism (1998) and Living Dolls (2010). Her life of activism is unsurprising, though, when you look at her family history. It’s in the blood. She tracks this zeal back through two generations, as she makes sense of her shock, grief and guilt at her mother’s suicide.
Aged 19, Ruth rejected her middle-class upbringing in north London suburbia. As a woman there were no expectations of university, only a future as “the perfect housewife”. Passionate, politically engaged and prepared to be arrested, Ruth — to her parents’ horror — gave up her Sainsbury’s job to become an activist.
On a “ban the bomb” march in 1960 she met Walter’s father, Nicolas, an Oxbridge-educated intellectual. The pair joined the radical Spies for Peace. In 1963 the group got a tip-off about a secret government bunker near Reading. After hours tramping over snowy fields, they found it. Astonishingly, it was unlocked. They had simply walked into a bunker built to shelter government officials in a nuclear war, containing plans for how the small elite would survive the apocalypse. They copied what they got into a pamphlet, which they posted to 3,000 influential people — celebrities, MPs, the media. There was a national outcry.
Stories like these are truly fascinating; Walter’s parents were key players. But theirs was not a great love story. “As individuals they were very different in very many ways,” Walter says. With two small daughters they scaled back the risk-taking and moved to a London suburb. Ruth became a social worker, got into radical feminism and divorced Nicolas.
But even more gripping — and tragic — is the story of Walter’s grandparents Georg and Eva. As a young communist in 1932 Georg took part in the anti-Nazi riots at Altona, in Hamburg. Eighteen people died. Georg was arrested, beaten, imprisoned without trial and found guilty of high treason. He spent two years at Fuhlsbüttel, a brutal concentration camp, before he finally escaped Nazi Germany hidden inside a crate in a coal train, breathing through a straw. In his seventies, with dementia, he would tell Ruth: “I ran through fire.”
He made it to Britain and in 1940 married Eva, a fellow Jewish refugee from Hamburg. Just 11 days after their wedding, though, they were swept off to separate British internment camps. By the time they were released a year later their campaigning souls were crushed. Georg became an accountant, Eva a brittle housewife.
The next generations took up the flame. Until she died Ruth was fit and active, a climate campaigner. Walter tried everything to cope with grief, but the only thing that has worked is more activism. In a police cell, having been arrested at an Extinction Rebellion protest, Walter realises that activism “looks like hope”. This rigorous, journalistic examination of an activist lineage is a powerful reminder — at a time when political protest often boils down to a tweet — that our actions really do matter.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre.title: Stuart Goldsmith at Edinburgh festival review — the funny side of climate change (yes, really)
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre.subtitle: Monkey Barrel Comedy
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre.text:
★★★★☆A funny show about climate change? One that punts neither complacency nor a disabling sense of all-is-lost alarm? Can such a thing be done? And is Stuart Goldsmith, a comedian who by his own admission has flown five times to New Zealand during the course of his comedy career and who has only in the past 18 months started boning up on the topic, really the man for the job?
Part of the quiet excellence of Goldsmith’s committed but adroitly unzealous show is the way he has fun with the idea of hypocrisy. He periodically polls his audience for our little eco sins and adds a few more of his own. We are all, he suggests with his customary affability, complicit in the carbon economy. So let’s take that as a given rather than use it as a gotcha. Let’s not do too much hand-wringing about those we accuse of hand-wringing.
OK, I haven’t made it sound a laugh riot. Yet much though Goldsmith owns up to his boy-scout tendencies, with the odd worrying stat or fact — fewer than you might expect — he keeps pretty much everything here draped in fun. He segues from the tortured etiquette of the WhatsApp group chat with fellow parents from his child’s school to his tortured attempts to keep up with his weekly email from Extinction Rebellion. The latter, he tells us, is from the “radical flank” of the movement — comparing the correspondence to the abrasive but necessary early work of the suffragettes, or of hip-hop before it became mainstream.
Goldsmith, by contrast, is a principled but mild-mannered comedian who has delved deep into his art through hundreds of episodes of his interview podcast The Comedian’s Comedian. He plies an intelligent, well-crafted act that can sometimes feel too clean-shaven, as if he were a man very ably playing the part of a comedian rather than a comedian in full contact with the moment. That sense abates, though, as he gets to grips with his subject and has fun with our worries about what to do next. Stuart Goldsmith: Spoilers is on until August 27, monkeybarrelcomedy.com

https://www.thetimes.com/article/man-det.title: Man detained after spending 24 hours on National Gallery roof
https://www.thetimes.com/article/man-det.subtitle: The gallery and Trafalgar Square were closed to the public after the man was spotted on Tuesday afternoon
https://www.thetimes.com/article/man-det.text:
A man has been detained after scaling the roof of the National Gallery and spending nearly 24 hours there.
The gallery in central London shut its doors and Trafalgar Square was closed to the public after he was spotted on the roof yesterday afternoon.
Police confirmed that the man had been detained under the Mental Health Act and that the gallery had reopened at noon.
The Metropolitan Police said: “Officers cordoned off and closed Trafalgar Square and surrounding roads, so at 3.45pm the decision was made to close the gallery to ensure the safety of our visitors and other members of the public. Summer on the Square was also closed.
“The incident continued throughout the night and part of following morning, with Trafalgar Square and the gallery remaining closed. At around 11.25am a man was detained under the Mental Health Act and taken to hospital.
“The gallery opened to visitors at around [noon], and Summer on the Square will open this afternoon. An investigation is now under way into how the man accessed the National Gallery roof.”
The National Gallery tweeted that the incident in Trafalgar Square has been “resolved”.
“The gallery is now open again and Summer on the Square will reopen from 12:30pm. If you had booked a free gallery entry ticket for a time during our temporary closure this morning, you are very welcome to visit us this afternoon without rebooking,” it said.
The gallery reported almost three million visits last year, according to the Art Newspaper. It is currently staging exhibitions about Francis of Assisi and post-impressionism.
Last year, the gallery became the target of environmental activists from the Just Stop Oil campaign, who threw tomato soup on Van Gogh’s Sunflowers. The painting was unharmed, but the frame suffered some minor damage.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: BBC star Chris Packham reported to police for sniffing goshawk chick
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
The TV presenter Chris Packham has been reported to police after he sniffed a wild chick on the BBC. The environmental campaigner was celebrating the return of goshawks, a bird of prey, to breed and was filmed on The One Show posing with three of their young.
Specialist rural crime officers are reviewing a possible offence under a law that treats goshawks as a protected species.
Packham, 62, has become a polarising figure with his support for Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion, along with his outspoken opposition to hunting and concerns about grouse shooting. Packham had promoted his appearance with the chicks on social media in June, writing: “Tonight on The One Show I get up close and very personal with some New Forest Goshawks!”
He was seen by millions of viewers sniffing a chick to experience its “characteristic scent or perfume” after the birds had been weighed, sexed and ringed in biometric tests. The complaint centres on whether the BBC had a licence in place to disturb rare species.
Goshawks may be removed from their nests for scientific and conservation purposes, and the ringer was operating under a permit issued by the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO). This allowed activities related to ringing, such as recording biometrics. Ringers are also permitted to photograph birds “provided that this causes no disturbance or any other harm”. Whether the filming caused any additional disturbance is difficult to measure but the BBC might have been able to request permission from Natural England, which is ultimately responsible for wildlife licensing. No such licence has been located, it is understood.
An amateur shooting enthusiast who complained to Hampshire police told The Times: “Licences are in place for the welfare of birds for a very good reason. Chris Packham was potentially disturbing the goshawks.”
The BBC is understood to consider that Packham was actively helping with the activities of ringing, measuring and weighing, all under trained supervision. The BBC’s position is that it did not interrupt or delay the professionals’ work.
The goshawk, also known as the tercel or tassel, used to be so common in England that it featured in Chaucer and several times in Shakespeare.
Packham lives in the New Forest, where a successful conservation programme has increased the number of goshawk pairs from one in 2002 to 45 now.
Goshawks are “raptors” like eagles. They are known as the “phantoms of the forest” because they are so elusive as they fly swiftly through the trees to swoop on prey.
Packham told the Sunday Telegraph: “Raptor persecution is illegal yet every year a huge number of goshawks are killed by gamekeepers . . . not by scientists or people in the media. All three of these birds fledged the nest — let’s hope they survive.”
Forestry England has placed a camera on one of the goshawk nests. The video made the surprising discovery that the male parent protected its young from the sun by spreading its wings to provide shade. Squirrels caught by the adult birds made up part of the chicks’ diet.
Andrew Stringer, head of environment and nature recovery for Forestry England, said: “All of the filming was carefully planned and overseen by a colleague with more than 35 years of experience and the birds’ welfare was always the priority.”
He said the organisation had not been contacted by the police and added: “This programme came along to film important work that we already had planned to do as part of a long-term scientific study and we had discussed it with the British Trust for Ornithology.”
Hampshire police said: “We received a report on July 2 relating to an alleged offence under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and it is currently being reviewed by our Countrywatch team.”
The BBC said: “The One Show had permission to film and followed all protocols around filming wildlife.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Labour’s Keir Mather: I often get, ‘Bloody hell, you’re young’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
I can’t deny I was well disposed towards Keir Mather, the fresh-minted, fresh-faced (at just 25, born in 1998, for goodness’ sake) Labour MP for Selby and Ainsty, even before we met. Like me, he’s from Hull, just 30-odd miles to the east, less if you grew up in the posh suburbs and villages to the west of Hull, as we both did.
He went to South Hunsley school, where my dad was once chairman of the governors and my niece and nephew were his contemporaries. I attended a neighbouring comprehensive with a similar demographic. His mum was a teacher. So was mine. His dad is a Labour activist. So was mine. We were both steeped in the East Yorkshire Labour movement from a young age. He knows local worthies who are the children of people I know, themselves the children of friends of my mum and dad.
I romanced my first girlfriend at the Omelette, the café opposite Hull Central Library run by his stepfather’s family for decades. Among young leftie sophisticates in Hull in the early Eighties, the Omelette was considered thrillingly exotic, largely because it was owned by Greek Cypriots, such was the deadening ethnic homogeneity of the city. Keir 2.0 and I also both went to Wadham College, Oxford, albeit 30 years apart. We even sound a bit alike, though my accent has worn off in a way his has not. You could say I know where he’s coming from.
I certainly know enough about the politics of the area to recognise that Mather’s victory, turning a Conservative majority of 20,000 into a Labour majority of 4,000 in the by-election a little over a fortnight ago, was sensational. His win was not about Labour rebuilding the red wall after 2019. This part of Yorkshire — like the prosperous roads where Mather and I grew up on Hull’s fringes — is historically overwhelmingly Tory. A Labour win here is hugely significant.
While my walk from Selby station traversed a high street hosting its share of charity shops, nail bars and tattoo parlours, such indications of deprivation are not representative of the constituency as a whole. Selby and Ainsty is home to mostly relatively well-off, well-qualified, mortgage-paying voters, commuting to Leeds and York from pretty villages and new-build estates. Mather’s triumph is the best indication yet that all sorts of voters now view the Labour Party as a credible alternative government. The swing can’t all be explained by animosity towards Nigel Adams, the retiring MP, who threw his toys out of the pram when he didn’t get his promised peerage.
• If we want young MPs they need help to survive• Charlotte Owen and Ross Kempsell: the curious rise of Johnson’s junior peers
We meet at Selby Town FC, average home attendance 300. Mather enthuses about a recent pre-season triumph over York City, then explains rugby (both codes) is more his game. He’s just broken a finger playing union and is a regular at Craven Park, home of rugby league’s Hull Kingston Rovers. Mather comes casually dressed, the outsized, borrowed-off-my-dad tweedy jacket of the by-election mercifully discarded. If he’s nervous about meeting the press, it doesn’t show. One advantage of interviewing a 25-year-old is that when the recorder on my phone malfunctions, he sorts it out in an instant.
After a brief gossip I’m relieved. I’d been dreading a robotic Lab-boy stooge and am thankful Mather isn’t one. On message (“Thirteen years of Tory decline”; “The Corbyn years were dark days for my party”). Earnest (“I’m going to work incredibly hard to repay the faith the voters have shown in me”). Keen on jargon (“future-focused”; “challenges”; “coalition of the willing”). Evasive on some issues (potential Ulez backtracking, transgender policy, Nigel Farage’s banking arrangements) for fear of saying the wrong thing. But, nonetheless, recognisably a sane, sensible 25-year-old, normal (whatever that is), genial and genuine, with a ready smile.
“Is this my ‘field of wheat’ question?” he jokes, in reference to Theresa May’s crop-trampling confession, when I ask if he had rebelled as a teenager. Ever got drunk? “Yeah.” Smoked? “I gave up a couple of years ago.” Vaped? “ ’Fraid so.” Drugs? “No. I smoked weed a couple of times. It was horrible.”
I apologise in advance that my questions will major on his childhood, but there isn’t much alternative, given the brevity of his adulthood. He smiles, already used to it. “Say what they like about my age, it doesn’t faze me.” Johnny Mercer, the veterans minister, has already been rude about his youth, likening him to a member of The Inbetweeners. Mather’s mum sprang to her son’s defence on Sky News, telling viewers how mature he was. Had he found the maternal intervention embarrassing? “No, I thought it was really sweet.” This is a guy who still gets ID’d in pubs. Did he get a lot of, “Bloody hell, you can’t be serious,” on the doorstep? “I got a lot of, ‘Bloody hell, you’re young.’ But I think people liked my energy and the way I was standing up to be counted.” Evidently, he is right.
I say there has been some controversy over his schooling that I’d like to clear up. Some sources claim he went to Hymers College, a fee-paying school, prior to enrolling at a comprehensive, and that during the by-election he, or his handlers, covered this up to emphasise his man-of-the-people credentials. Bearing in mind I know chapter and verse about the Hull and East Riding education set-up, I warn him, here’s his chance to come clean. “You want the full timeline, right?” he says. Sure do, I reply.
“I lived in Hull until I was about 10 or 11,” he starts. Where? “The Parade, off Cave Street, near Princes Avenue.” I know it well. “I did three years of primary at St Vincent’s,” he reports. Is he Catholic? “No, but they let me in. Then my mum worked extremely hard and managed to get me into Froebel House, which is private. Do you know it?” Of course, I say. “I was there for three years, then we moved out to Brough [a large and expanding village ten miles away] and I went to Elloughton primary for Year 6. Then to South Hunsley for my entire secondary school. No Hymers at all.”
It’s worth getting into the weeds of this, I reckon. Partly because the state/private divide in Britain remains hugely significant, whatever some people (who usually went to private school and are seeking to downplay the advantages it confers) claim. And partly because Mather will, I think, one day become a major player in our politics (he’s already been mentioned as a future Labour leader, albeit mostly so far by his mum), so it’s good to get the facts of his education straight.
• Labour will need more Keirs like this new one• Rishi Sunak aims to divide and rule after poll setback
How would he, I ask, mining the same vein, characterise his class background? He offers an impressively nuanced answer. “My class identity, like a lot of people’s in the UK, is complicated and contested. My mum’s dad was a captain in the Merchant Navy. They were industrious, aspirational, small ‘c’ conservative. My dad’s side were from Tyneside. His dad was a shipbuilder.” (Mather has applied to join the Royal Navy Reserve, like Penny Mordaunt, in homage to both grandfathers. He was due to start officer training but the by-election intervened.) “As a kid, I went to birthday parties on Tyneside in places with the banner from the local pit on the wall. So I grew up in the Labour movement tradition and the northern aspirational tradition as well.” The preferences of this second tradition will go a long way towards deciding the next election.
Mather’s mum and dad, both university graduates (Leicester and Newcastle respectively), worked as careers advisers when he was a boy. They split up when he was about nine and maintain a good relationship. “I see my dad all the time. He now works for Hull City Council.” His mum, Jill, became a supply teacher for a while and now works with her second husband, George Tambaros, scion of the Omelette owners, in his property services business. He has a younger brother, Zak, 22. “He’s finding this all a bit surreal, like a lot of my family.”
Mather admits, unsurprisingly, “I’ve always been into politics.” Yet he denies he was any sort of a nerd as a kid, even when I encourage him by saying I was, and there’s no shame in it. His dad was and is a strong Labour man — hence naming his son in honour of James Keir Hardie, Labour’s first parliamentary leader — yet his mum, Mather insists, is “a non-committed swing voter”. He dimly remembers Gordon Brown as prime minister, but he does not recall any strong emotion at Labour’s defeat in 2010, when he was 12. “I was engaged by then, but not obsessive.”
Even later on, as his enthusiasm developed through his teens, he was never known, he says, as the weird kid always banging on about politics. “I had other interests, a run of the mill school experience, a normal childhood kicking about with friends. Going to watch Rovers. The pub. Skateboarding. Regular stuff.”
Aged 18, having known he was gay for some time, he came out to his parents. “It’s always an enormous thing for anyone to come out to their family, but I knew how much my parents loved and respected me and I knew fundamentally it wasn’t gonna be an issue. And it wasn’t. I was extremely lucky.” He is in a relationship now but declines to go into detail. He thinks homophobia is on the rise, yet has rarely experienced it himself. “A few shouts from a car when I was younger,” he recalls. Does he hold hands with his boyfriend in Hull? “Absolutely. I’m confident.”
His passion for politics led to his mum ferrying him around Hull to visit the city’s three Labour MPs, asking their advice on setting up a young Labour group. “They were pleased someone was keen.” Former home secretary Alan Johnson spoke at the group’s inaugural meeting. Did the young Mather have a careerist agenda, as one or two contemporaries have alleged? “I always saw being an MP as the most incredible opportunity,” he replies. “I always said that it would be a phenomenal job to do and, if I got the opportunity, it would be the privilege of my life.” I take that as a yes to having had half a networking eye on future preferment. Which is fair enough, in my view. I’ve never understood why wanting to be a professional politician is seen as an ignoble ambition. Quite the opposite.
He did well academically and was fortunate that his teachers encouraged his Oxford application. That is not always the case at northern comprehensives. “There was no well-established culture of going there, but my teachers refused to accept that pupils from schools like ours couldn’t go to the best university in the UK.” Did he have an, ahem, “Gap Yah”? “I did not. I’m not from that sort of family. It wouldn’t have occurred to me in a million years.”
He admits to some culture shock when first arriving at Oxford. “It’s intimidating, yeah. I remember when I got my offer a friend of mine joking, ‘Oh, shouldn’t you be down the mines?’ It was a throwaway comment, but it did make me think, ‘What are you getting into here?’ You arrive, you don’t know anyone. You don’t realise how geography and social class manifest themselves. Why do all these people seem so confident? With hindsight, I know there were lots of people there from families and schools where they’re trained to feel confident in these environments.”
For youngsters from his background, the first term at Oxford (like any university, but maybe more so, given that for most of its history this institution has not welcomed those who do not fit a certain profile) is sink or swim. He decided to swim. “My fear was offset by excitement. I thought, ‘I’ve got to grab this and give it all the energy I’ve got.’ ” Did he get any hassle for his accent? “I was teased a bit about where I was from. There was also that, ‘You managed to get here. Isn’t that incredible!’ attitude.”
Let’s get back to his extreme youth, I say. He laughs dutifully. He’s Gen Z, isn’t he? “Am I?” Yes, you are, I tell him, so let’s run the stereotype by you. Vegetarian? “No, I’m not.” Ever kissed a Tory? “Er, probably.” Glastonbury? “Never been. I’ve been to Leeds Fest though.” Just Stop Oil: pain in the arse? “Yeah, they are. It is bloody arrogant to think you have the sole means to impact this debate. I cannot see the utility in consistently pissing people off.” Does he reckon Angela Rayner is going to have a quiet word with Sadiq Khan after the Ulez debacle in Uxbridge? “London’s not my patch,” he dodges.
At Oxford, did he really call Germaine Greer “an abhorrent transphobe” for saying trans women weren’t really women? He flannels. “It’s half a decade ago now. The debate was extremely hot; I can’t remember the context.” He goes on about kindness and empathy. “On the question of, ‘What is a woman?’ a woman is like my mum or my stepsister, somebody who is born biologically a woman. But there is a very small minority of people who feel like they’ve been born into the wrong gender and they deserve respect and care.” Does he now wish to repudiate what he said about Greer, bearing in mind Sir Keir Starmer seems finally to have decided that a woman can’t have a penis? “What I said is on the record. I really strongly disagree with her outlook and approach to the issue.”
During the campaign, Mather commuted from his mum’s house in Brough. He’d been living in London — “paying through the nose for my rent in a flatshare” — but is moving to Selby imminently. “I can’t wait to get cracking.” He badly needs to pass his driving test, having failed three times. Elected on the day the House rose for summer recess, Mather hasn’t yet sampled the reportedly toxic atmosphere of his new workplace. The abuse, the boozing, the late nights, the travel, the harassment — Mhairi Black, his predecessor as “the baby of the House”, has had enough and is stepping down. But he won’t, he says, be intimidated. Cold electoral logic suggests he’ll almost certainly get turfed out at the general election. But even if he does, I think we will hear more of this young man.
