https://www.thetimes.com/article/profess.title: Stop parading your politics, Alex Chalk tells lawyers
https://www.thetimes.com/article/profess.text:
The justice secretary told lawyers to stop “parading their politics” as the government stepped up its attack on legal firms helping to frustrate attempts to crack down on illegal immigration.
Alex Chalk said there was a “regrettable trend” of lawyers in the UK being willing to identify more with the cause of their clients. He told lawyers to “keep their politics to themselves” and said they should avoid becoming involved in political opposition to government policy.
He made the comments after about 20 migrants refused to be moved on to the Bibby Stockholm barge in Portland Port in Dorset on Monday after the refugee charity Care4Calais and lawyers from the Duncan Lewis law firm made individual legal challenges to their transfer.
On Tuesday Carralyn Parkes, the Labour mayor of Portland, made a separate legal challenge to the use of the barge to accommodate migrants. Her case argues that planning permission to berth the vessel in the port was “neither sought nor granted”.
Her legal case, submitted on her behalf by Deighton Pierce Glynn solicitors, which specialises in civil rights and judicial reviews, also argues that the barge is in effect a permanent structure that is dependent on supplies of electricity, sewage treatment and local staff. In a statement, Deighton Pierce Glynn said: “The home secretary is circumventing planning permission procedures to use the Bibby Stockholm barge to accommodate vulnerable asylum seekers in conditions which are clearly inadequate.
“The home secretary’s plans have caused widespread concern in our client’s local community, and have deprived the council of its ability to exert relevant planning control. We will be asking the court to declare that planning permission is required, and that the home secretary must follow the relevant procedures.”
The Home Office has said that it is a private port, which does not require the same planning permission as using public land, and that it is providing “substantial funding to local services to address the local community’s concerns”.
Chalk, right, said that he found it frustrating that only 15 people had been moved on to the barge on Monday, despite the Home Office telling a further 20 people of their intention to transfer them. The Home Office has threatened those who refuse to be moved on to the barge with having their accommodation support withdrawn altogether. Their asylum claim may also be delayed or cancelled entirely if they continue to resist.
Several more migrants were seen being moved on to the barge, which will eventually house up to 506 migrants, on Tuesday. They did not include the group of 20 who refused to be transferred on Monday.
Chalk accepted that lawyers had a right to submit legal challenges to government policy, telling the BBC: “The government is frustrated, of course, by legal challenges, those legal challenges are not improper of themselves, but we will be challenging them because we take the view that they are misguided, they’re wrong-headed, they’re last minute, they’re completely misconceived and we will be challenging them in the normal way.”
Suggesting that they were part of a growing trend of lawyers pursuing a political cause, Chalk added: “The strong tradition of lawyers in this country is that you simply act for your client without fear or favour and you don’t necessarily associate yourself with that cause. But I think it is fair to point out that in the last ten years there has been a growing, and I think regrettable, trend for lawyers to actively parade their politics and to identify more with their clients.• Small boat smugglers targeted in intelligence deal with Turkey
“I think if they can avoid that they should avoid it. It’s much better, I think, in the main, to keep their politics to themselves and to simply do their job on behalf of their clients, but some seem to be much more willing and in some cases enthusiastic about parading their political opposition, and I think that’s a mistake.”
Chalk, who replaced Dominic Raab as justice secretary in April, also defended controversial comments by Lee Anderson, the Conservative Party deputy chairman, who said asylum seekers complaining about the Bibby Stockholm barge should “f*** off back to France”.
The minister told LBC: “Lee Anderson expresses the righteous indignation of the British people. Yes, he does it in salty terms, that’s his style, but his indignation is well placed.”
The lord chancellor may have had several people in mind when telling lawyers to “keep their politics to themselves” (Jonathan Ames writes).
This tax law specialist has opinions by the barrel-load. A passionate anti-Brexiteer, he launched the Good Law Project and the Good Law Practice. His 425,000 followers are routinely treated to Maugham’s opinions on subjects far beyond his initial Brexit bugbear, such as climate change, transgender rights, the government’s performance in the pandemic and the state of the Labour Party leadership.
A Cambridge University graduate who is an unashamed tree-hugger. His three-piece suits are a concession to professional convention; his long hair in a messy bun keeps him sweet with the likes of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil. In 2020, he said that he believes that forests and rivers should have legal rights and that he once accepted trees as payment of his fees.
A solicitor at the prominent civil liberties London law firm Birnberg Peirce, his father was the renowned and highly respected journalist Paul Foot. He is also related to the former Labour leader Michael Foot. He co-founded Justice Alliance, which ten years ago he described as being a “coalition of legal and non-legal organisations, community groups and charities”.
Another legal profession star on Twitter. In common with Maugham, Simor is an arch Remainer — in 2019 she stood as a candidate in London in the EU parliament elections for Change UK, a pro-EU party.
Asylum seekers who spent their first night on the Bibby Stockholm have said the barge accommodation is “good”, as they began to explore the local area (Will Humphries writes).
Only 15 asylum seekers moved on to the barge on the first day of arrivals after weeks of delays caused by repair work, health and safety concerns and warnings of the vessel being a fire trap. Several asylum seekers used the free hourly coach paid for by the Home Office to take them the six miles from the secure private port in Portland to Weymouth town centre.
An Algerian asylum seeker, 31, who did not wish to give his name, was the only man to get off the coach in Weymouth at 1.30pm. He said the barge was “fine” and the food and bed “good”.
The 222-room, three-storey barge arrived in Portland Port three weeks ago, chartered by the government to reduce the cost of placing asylum seekers in hotels. It has been retrofitted to accommodate about 500 adult men.
Amnesty International has compared the Bibby Stockholm to “prison hulks from the Victorian era”, saying it was an “utterly shameful way to house people who’ve fled terror, conflict and persecution”.
English classes will be held twice a week on the barge, as well as cultural courses that will teach them how to fit into British life. The migrants are free to come and go from the barge but are being “strongly encouraged” to return to it by 11pm. On arrival, migrants are given a security key card for their rooms and other spaces so their movements can be tracked.
The Home Office said conditions on the barge were safe and appropriate.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Security warning after Greenpeace stunt at Rishi Sunak’s home
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: A former terrorism tsar said it showed ‘a serious lapse of attention’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Greenpeace’s ability to “invade” Rishi Sunak’s home to protest about the government’s North Sea oil strategy represented an “astonishing” breach of security, the government’s former counter terrorism advisor has warned.
In a letter to The Times, Lord Carlile of Berriew said the group should never have been able to access the site and that their ability to do so demonstrated a “failure of surveillance and a serious lapse of attention”.
He also called on the group’s charitable arm — that provides Greenpeace with over £2 million of funding each year — to “reflect” on what had happened or risk imperilling the organisation’s charitable status.
“Targeting a politician’s private residence is an intimidatory act by those who have not troubled to achieve their policies through the electoral process,” he said. “Greenpeace’s trustees should have cause to reflect on what occurred, not least because I assume that they do not wish to imperil the organisation’s charitable status.”
Lord Carlile’s comments came as Downing Street said Greenpeace would no longer be given a “seat at the table” in government discussions about climate change and other environmental issues following the stunt.• Read the letter in full
Five Greenpeace activists were arrested after climbing onto the roof of Sunak’s grade II listed North Yorkshire constituency home last week and draping it in black to “drive home the dangerous consequences of a new drilling frenzy”.
On Monday the prime minister’s official spokesman said all government departments should suspend stakeholder engagement with Greenpeace. “Certainly we obviously don’t think that people who are accused of breaking the law should have a seat at the table in discussions with government,” the prime minister’s spokesman said.
“Clearly given their actions and the arrests last week we don’t think it’s appropriate to engage with them.”
Security sources are understood to have had concerns that although Sunak was away at the time any intruder who had access to the building could still pose a significant potential threat to the prime minister and his family.
In his letter Carlile said he had “long respected Greenpeace and counterterrorism policing” but now found himself “disappointed with both and anxious about their directions of travel”.
“As a former independent reviewer of terrorism legislation for the UK I am astonished that protesters were able to trespass at length on the prime minister’s private home,” he said. “This demonstrates a failure of surveillance and a serious lapse of attention.”
He added: “Concerning the Greenpeace Environmental Trust, as a UK registered charity they should have regarded it as ethically unsound for Greenpeace Limited, which it funded to the extent of £2.4 million last year, to invade the family home of an elected representative.”
A spokesman for the Charity Commission said: “All charities must ensure their spending furthers exclusively charitable purposes/activities, including when funding or supporting non-charitable organisations.
“If we receive evidence or concerns that a charity’s funds are being misused for non-charitable activity, we will assess that to determine our next steps.”
Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace, defended the protest as “carefully and meticulously” planned for when the prime minister, his wife and children were on holiday in California.
She told Sky News it was a “proportionate response to a disastrous decision” by Sunak to allow for further drilling.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/jami.title: Jamie Reid obituary
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/jami.subtitle: Artist and anarchist whose décollage aesthetic became the house style of the Sex Pistols at the vanguard of the punk insurrection
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/jami.text:
Jamie Reid was in the Outer Hebrides when he first learnt about the punk insurrection that was soon to burst messily over the 1970s like an angry rash.
News of the gathering storm came in a telegram from Malcolm McLaren, asking Reid to return to London because he needed a visual artist whose iconoclasm could match the seditious clamour and rabble-rousing noise of the band he was about to launch on an unsuspecting world. The band were called the Sex Pistols.
Reid and McLaren were old friends who had met as students at Croydon College of Art in late 1968 and shared an interest in anarchy and dissent. However, while McLaren opened his famous shop, Sex, with Vivienne Westwood on Chelsea’s Kings Road, Reid’s subversion had followed a different course and in 1975 he abandoned London to try his hand at crofting on a remote Scottish island.
By then he had already developed a distinctive style as a graphic artist that involved cutting letters out from newspaper headlines in the style of an anonymous ransom note and using them to superimpose transgressive messages on incongruous images.
It was a technique that captured the DIY, up-yours essence of punk as quintessentially as the sneering voice of Johnny Rotten and Reid immediately set to work on producing a poster to promote the Sex Pistols’ first single, Anarchy in the UK (1976), with the band’s name and the title of the song in cut-up letters attached by safety pins to a torn and tattered Union Jack.
For the picture sleeve of the follow-up single God Save The Queen, he took a Cecil Beaton photographic portrait of Queen Elizabeth II and defaced it, covering her eyes in swastikas and putting a safety pin through her mouth.
Released just in time to pour scorn on the Queen’s Silver Jubilee in 1977, the record was banned by the BBC and shops refused to display Reid’s cover art.
On June 7, 1977, the Jubilee holiday, McLaren hired a boat named the Queen Elizabeth on the Thames and the Sex Pistols hammered out a seething version of the banned song as they cruised past the Palace of Westminster.
The boat was swiftly encircled by police launches with searchlights and a megaphone and ordered back to Charing Cross pier, where Reid and McLaren were among 11 people who were arrested. Reid recalled “being wrestled to the ground by Special Patrol Group riot police and seeing through the mayhem Steve Jones, the Pistols guitarist, lobbing a can of beer at the police”.
Even better, from his cell he was delighted to hear a bunch of football hooligans banged up for a quite different misdemeanour raucously singing God Save The Queen — not the official national anthem but “our version”.
A quarter of a century later, Reid’s artwork for the single was voted No 1 in a list of the 100 greatest record covers by Q magazine. A copy is also in the National Portrait Gallery’s collection.
For the Sex Pistols’ third single, Pretty Vacant, Reid designed a smashed empty picture frame and then produced a doctored comic strip for their fourth single, Holidays in the Sun.
He also designed the cover for the band’s album, with the title Never Mind The Bollocks Here’s The Sex Pistols, picked out in the style of a ransom note on a yellow and pink DayGlo background.
The album went to No 1 but record shops up and down the country were ordered by police not to exhibit Reid’s artwork in their window displays. When the manager of the Nottingham branch of Virgin Records continued to display the cover he was arrested and prosecuted for obscenity. John Mortimer, hired as QC for the defence, argued that double standards were at play for the word “bollocks” only seemed to be considered obscene when it appeared on the cover of a Sex Pistols album. The hapless shop manager was acquitted on four separate charges.
The Sex Pistols soon burnt out and broke up just two and a half months after the release of the album. At their final gig in San Francisco in January 1978, Rotten told the audience: “Ah-ha-ha. Ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated?” before he walked offstage.
Punk fizzled out too but Reid’s subversive mission remained undimmed. In later years he used his art to further a variety of radical causes and protest movements, waging visual war on the poll tax and the Criminal Justice Bill and more recently supporting Occupy, Extinction Rebellion and the campaign to free Pussy Riot, the all-female Russian band imprisoned by President Putin.
One of his most striking later works was a 1991 painting of John Wayne with a CND symbol painted on his cowboy hat and his sheriff’s badge doctored to read “Peace is tough”. Later still, a series of screen prints he produced in 1997 to mark the 20th anniversary of God Save The Queen, adapted the original design with the slogan “Never Trust a Punk”.
Regarding himself as one of the last of Robespierre’s sea-green incorruptibles, he was sharply critical of the big money surrounding the Damien Hirst/Tracy Emin school of Britart, dismissing them as “Thatcher’s children”.
When Hirst threatened to sue a student for copyright infringement he denounced him as a “hypocritical and greedy art bully” and produced a riff on his “God Save The Queen” image with the words “God Save Damien Hirst”. Even Banksy, who would appear to be a natural comrade-in-arms, was accused of “cheap tricks”.
Reid’s own work developed into colourful abstracts, absorbing African influences and astrological and druidic imagery and can be found in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Victoria and Albert Museum and Tate Gallery in London.
He is survived by his daughter Rowan from a long-term relationship with his former partner, the Liverpudlian actress Margi Clarke, best known for her leading role in the 1985 film Letter To Brezhnev and the late-night ITV show The Good Sex Guide.
Jamie Reid was born in 1947 and grew up in a bohemian enclave in Croydon in the heart of south London suburbia. His parents were “diehard socialists” and his great uncle was George Watson MacGregor Reid, a druid who established and led the Church of the Universal Bond, dedicated to socialist revolution, anti-imperialism and sun worship.
He called himself a “socialist druid” — albeit with a streak of anarchism — and was an honorary bard in the Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids.
At John Ruskin Grammar School in Croydon he fell under the influence of a sympathetic art teacher who recommended him for a place at Wimbledon College of Art, which he took up at the age of 15. Two years later he transferred to Croydon College of Art, where he met McLaren. The two declared themselves to be followers of the Situationist manifesto of the French philosopher Guy Debord, whose theories about the decay of capitalism heavily inspired the student revolts which swept Paris and other European cities in 1968. Reid and McLaren organised their own sit-ins in solidarity.
After graduating, in 1970 Reid co-founded the magazine Suburban Press, a radical left-wing publication partly rooted in Debord’s political philosophy. It was in the pages of the magazine that he developed the décollage style of cut-out words and images that McClaren identified as the visual embodiment of the iconoclastic sound of punk rock.
The magazine ran until 1975 and circulation never rose above 5,000 but it was a vital grounding, not only for the free range Reid had in its pages but for the lesson it offered on the ins and outs of printing. “A lot of the work with the Sex Pistols was a result of what I’d learnt on that press,” he said.
In the 1980s he moved to Liverpool where he taught art to children off the street at a local community centre. For many years he also maintained a studio at Whitechapel in London’s East End.
On his death his gallerist John Marchant described him as an “artist, iconoclast, anarchist, punk, hippie, rebel and romantic”, while his own website described his work as blending “gnosticism and dissent”.
Reid was dismayed but not surprised by the rightward drift of contemporary politics and in 2017 he reworked his swastika-eyed God Save The Queen artwork to target Donald Trump with the legend “God Save Us All”.
His spirit remained transgressive until the end. “When God Save The Queen got to No 1 it proved there was genuine opposition to what was going on,” he said 40 years on. “The trouble is that the people in control have made sure it will never happen again.”
Jamie Reid, artist and activist, was born on January 16, 1947. He died of unknown causes on August 8, 2023, aged 76
